clinicalPearls: A chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with papillary necrosis caused by prolonged heavy analgesic use, historically phenacetin-containing combinations
Cumulative dose over many years is the key exposure, and combination analgesics are more nephrotoxic than single agents
Classically described in middle-aged women with chronic pain, headaches or psychiatric comorbidity and a habit of daily analgesic use
It presents insidiously with impaired urinary concentration, sterile pyuria, modest proteinuria, hypertension and slowly progressive renal impairment
Papillary necrosis may cause haematuria or colic when a papilla sloughs
CT typically shows small, scarred kidneys with bumpy contours and papillary calcification
There is an increased long-term risk of urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma, so urine cytology surveillance is warranted
The essential treatment is to stop all offending analgesics, after which renal decline may stabilise
reference.pathophysiology: Long-term ingestion of analgesic mixtures damages the renal medulla by two complementary mechanisms. Phenacetin and its metabolite paracetamol accumulate and generate oxidative injury in the papillary tissue, while aspirin depletes protective prostaglandins, reducing medullary blood flow, and depletes glutathione, potentiating the toxicity. The medulla, already functioning at low oxygen tension, sustains combined ischaemic and oxidative damage leading to papillary necrosis and a surrounding chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Over years this produces shrunken, scarred kidneys, and chronic urothelial injury predisposes to transitional cell carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis such as lithium, lead or aristolochic acid (Chinese-herb) nephropathy
additionalInvestigations: A careful analgesic and drug history quantifying cumulative use
CT showing small kidneys with an irregular outline and papillary calcification
Urinalysis for sterile pyuria and low-grade proteinuria
Renal function and assessment of urinary concentrating ability
Urine cytology to screen for urothelial malignancy
Cross-sectional imaging or cystoscopy if malignancy is suspected
redFlags: New or persistent haematuria raising concern for urothelial carcinoma
Progressive renal impairment despite stopping analgesics
Acute obstruction with infection from a sloughed papilla
reference.prognosis: If analgesic use stops early, renal function often stabilises; continued use leads to progressive chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure, and a lifelong risk of urothelial cancer persists even after cessation.
pitfalls: Not taking a detailed over-the-counter analgesic history, so the cause is missed
Allowing the patient to continue nephrotoxic analgesics for chronic pain
Overlooking urothelial malignancy when haematuria develops
Attributing the picture to hypertension alone rather than to analgesic injury
management: Cease all analgesic use permanently, particularly combination analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, as the key disease-modifying step
Provide alternative pain strategies and address the underlying chronic pain, headache and psychiatric comorbidity that drive analgesic use
Manage the chronic kidney disease with blood pressure control and general nephroprotective measures
Monitor renal function and urinary concentrating ability over time
Undertake lifelong surveillance for urothelial malignancy with urine cytology, and imaging or cystoscopy where suspected
Refer to nephrology and urology, and provide renal replacement therapy if end-stage failure develops
